title: Functional Java
goal: Lambdas, functional interfaces, Streams aur Optional se data pipelines banana.
objectives: Write lambdas against the right functional interface
Build a stream pipeline with intermediate and terminal operations
Use collect, reduce and Optional without null checks everywhere
Explain when a parallel stream helps and when it hurts
definition: A lambda is an anonymous function assigned to a functional interface. The Stream API processes a sequence declaratively: intermediate operations (filter, map, sorted) are lazy and return a new stream, and a terminal operation (collect, forEach, reduce, count) triggers the work exactly once.
explain: A functional interface has one abstract method, so the compiler can infer the lambda's shape: Predicate<T> is T → boolean, Function<T,R> is T → R, Consumer<T> is T → void, Supplier<T> is () → T. Method references (String::length) are shorthand when an existing method already fits.

Streams are lazy: filter and map describe work, but nothing runs until a terminal operation asks for a result. That lets the implementation fuse steps and stop early with findFirst. A stream can be consumed once; reusing it throws IllegalStateException.

collect(Collectors.toList()), groupingBy and joining turn streams back into collections and strings. Optional models a value that may be absent, forcing you to handle the empty case instead of risking a NullPointerException. Parallel streams split work across threads but only pay off for large, CPU-bound, easily splittable work — and they must not touch shared mutable state.
hinglish: Functional interface me ek abstract method hota hai, isliye lambda ka shape compiler infer kar leta hai: Predicate T→boolean, Function T→R, Consumer T→void, Supplier ()→T. Method reference tab use karo jab koi existing method exactly fit ho.

Stream lazy hai: filter/map sirf describe karte hain, kaam tab hota hai jab terminal operation aata hai. Ek stream sirf ek baar consume hoti hai — dobara use karoge to IllegalStateException. Optional absent value ko represent karta hai, taaki null checks ki jagah explicit handling ho.
analogy: Stream ek assembly line hai: filter ek quality-check station, map ek transformation station, aur collect truck hai jo end par maal uthata hai. Jab tak truck nahi aata, line start hi nahi hoti — isliye laziness se kaam bachta hai.
why: Modern Java codebases read like stream pipelines, and interviews test whether you know laziness, collectors and Optional. Writing a loop is fine, but knowing when a pipeline is clearer and safer is a senior-level signal.

syntax.note: Each step returns a new stream; collect is the terminal operation that runs the pipeline.
findFirst returns Optional. orElse gives a fallback; map transforms only when a value is present.

topics.title: Lambdas and functional interfaces
topics.body: A lambda is (params) -> expression or a block. It implements a functional interface. @FunctionalInterface documents and enforces the single-method rule. Lambdas capture effectively final locals only.

topics.title: The four core interfaces
topics.body: Predicate<T> (test), Function<T,R> (apply), Consumer<T> (accept), Supplier<T> (get). BiFunction, UnaryOperator, BiConsumer and primitive specialisations (IntPredicate, ToIntFunction) avoid boxing in hot code.

topics.title: Method references
topics.body: Four forms: Type::staticMethod, instance::method, Type::instanceMethod (on a parameter) and Type::new. Use one when the lambda would only forward its argument.

topics.title: Stream sources and intermediate operations
topics.body: Sources: collection.stream(), Arrays.stream, Stream.of, Files.lines, IntStream.range. Intermediate: filter, map, flatMap, distinct, sorted, limit, skip, peek. They are lazy and may be reordered by the implementation.

topics.title: Terminal operations and collecting
topics.body: Terminal: forEach, count, anyMatch/allMatch/noneMatch, findFirst, reduce, collect, toList. Collectors.toList/toSet/toMap, joining, groupingBy, partitioningBy, counting, summingInt cover most reporting needs.

topics.title: Optional
topics.body: Optional<T> is a container that may be empty. Use map/flatMap/filter/orElse/orElseGet/orElseThrow/ifPresent. Do not use it for fields or method parameters in most designs, and never call get() without checking.

topics.title: Parallel streams and performance
topics.body: parallelStream splits work with the common ForkJoinPool. It helps for large CPU-bound independent work and hurts for small data, I/O, ordered output or shared mutable state. Measure before claiming a speedup.

examples.title: Filter, map, sort and collect
lines: filter keeps names starting with A: Aman and Anita.
map converts each to upper case and sorted orders them alphabetically.
mapToInt avoids boxing and summaryStatistics reports the maximum length (Priya, 5).
groupingBy counts names by their first character, giving A=2, P=1, R=1.
dryRun: Priya filtered out; Ravi filtered out; Anita → ANITA
Max length = 5; grouping counts by first letter

examples.title: Optional, map and reduce
lines: parse returns Optional.empty for invalid text instead of throwing to the caller.
flatMap(Optional::stream) drops the empty optionals and keeps the numbers.
orElse supplies -1 for the invalid value, and map doubles the present 7 to 14.

mistakes.right: Use each stream once; recreate it with list.stream() for a second pass.
mistakes.why: A stream is consumed by its terminal operation; reusing it throws IllegalStateException.
A lambda may not modify a local variable, and shared mutable state breaks under parallel streams. Use reduce or a collector.

debug.brief: This pipeline is meant to print the count of even numbers, but throws IllegalStateException. Fix the reuse.
hints: count() is a terminal operation and consumes the stream.
Create the pipeline twice, or collect it once and reuse the list.

best: Keep pipelines short; extract a named method when a step needs a comment.
Prefer mapToInt/mapToDouble for numeric work to avoid boxing.
Return Optional from search methods, not null.
Measure before parallelising; shared mutable state makes it wrong, not just slow.
tip: When asked 'why are streams lazy?', connect it to short-circuiting: findFirst on an infinite stream can finish because intermediate steps only run when the terminal asks. Then mention that a stream is single-use.
revision: Lambda implements a functional interface; method reference is shorthand.
Intermediate operations are lazy; a terminal operation runs the pipeline.
collect/Collectors turn results back into collections and strings.
Optional models absence; parallel only for large independent CPU work.

practice.title: Long names
practice.prompt: From a list of names, print the upper-cased names longer than 4 characters, sorted.

practice.title: Group by length
practice.prompt: Group words by their length and print each length with its words.

practice.title: Optional chain

mcqs.explain: collect consumes the stream and produces a result; the others are lazy intermediate steps.
test(T) returns a boolean, which is why filter takes a Predicate.

mcqs.q: What happens when you reuse a consumed stream?
mcqs.explain: Streams are single-use; the second terminal operation throws IllegalStateException.

interview.q: Stream vs for loop — when do you use which?
interview.a: Streams read better for filter/map/group pipelines and are easy to parallelise, but have overhead and can obscure index-dependent or stateful logic. A loop is clearer for early exits with complex control flow or for hot inner loops. Choose the readable one and measure if performance matters.
interview.followUp: Are streams always slower? (Not necessarily; for large data the difference is small, and parallel streams can win — measure.)

interview.q: What is Optional for, and what is it not for?
interview.a: Optional is a return type that makes absence explicit and composable. It is not a general null replacement: avoid it for fields, method parameters and collections, and never call get() without a presence check.
interview.followUp: Optional.of vs ofNullable? (of throws on null; ofNullable returns empty.)

lab.title: Sum of squares of evens
lab.brief: Read n then n integers. Print the sum of the squares of the even numbers, using a stream.
hints: mapToInt avoids boxing and gives sum() directly.

checkpoint.title: Pipelines readable and correct?
checks: I can name the four core functional interfaces and their shapes
I know which operations are lazy and which run the pipeline
I never reuse a stream or mutate shared state in a lambda
